fields.name: search_knowledge_vector
fields.description:
PRIMARY KNOWLEDGE SEARCH TOOL.
          Use this for ANY question about 'Who', 'What', 'Where', 'Ownership', or 'Concepts' stored in the system.
          It uses Vector Search + GraphRAG to find nodes AND their relationships (e.g. "Who owns X").
          Finds: Companies, Websites, Code, Concepts, and their connections.

fields.name: search_project_memory

Search THIS PROJECT'S saved memory/knowledge (Vector + GraphRAG).
          Use for anything the user or their team saved to project memory:
          project-specific preferences, decisions, snippets and facts.
          ALWAYS pass the projectId from your context. This complements
          search_knowledge_vector, which searches the GLOBAL built-in docs.

List ALL saved memory entries for THIS PROJECT (newest first),
          each with its 'id', 'label' and properties. Use this to show the user
          their project memory, or to find the 'id' of an entry you then want to

fields.name: search_graph
fields.description:
Search the knowledge graph. You can provide either a plain-text query (e.g. "Lambda environment configurations") or a Cypher query. For plain text, it searches across node name, content, description, and text fields.

  Schema:
  (:User {idString})
  (:Chat {idString, createdAtNumber})
  (:Message {idString, roleString, contentString, createdAtNumber})
  (User)-[:OWNS]->(Chat)
  (Chat)-[:HAS_MESSAGE]->(Message)
  (Message)-[:NEXT]->(Message)

  AND Dynamic Knowledge Nodes created via add_knowledge:
  (:Concept {name, id}), (:Fact {name, id}), (:Entity {name, id}), (:Company {name, id}), etc.
  Relationships are dynamic.
  Use plain text to search, or a Cypher query for advanced queries.

types.name: FissionEnvironmentType
types.description:
Functions defined inside an environment "pool" with type "poolmgr" are relying on scale options defined in the pool itself
  Functions defined as "newdeploy" are using only the image from the pool for execution and scale options are defined in the function itself
  
  Scale options description:
  (minMemory, maxMemory, minCpu, maxCpu) used per pod inside the pool usable for functions with type poolmgr aka pool managed scalability

  IMPORTANT: type FissionEnvironmentInputType has the same description

fields.name: projectId
fields.description: Project namespace where this environment is attached

fields.name: name
fields.description: Name of the environment by default is "nodejs" but it can be any text

fields.name: image
fields.description: The environment docker image in which functions will be runned against, default one is "rxdi/fission-node:0.0.5"

fields.name: builder
fields.description: The environment builder image in which packages and builds will be runned for a function in this pool

fields.name: poolSize
fields.description:
How many active pods will remain waiting for a function execution.
      Keep in mind they are long lived and will remain running and consume CPU and memory
      If pool size is set to 0 function pods relying on "poolmgr" will not be working! 
      If pool size is set to 0 function pods relying on "newdeploy", will use only the builder image and will spawn a new deploy when function is runned
      If "newdeploy" is set ALWAYS set the poolSize to 0 since we don't need running pods
      If "newdeploy" is set but this pool is used by functions with "poolmgr" there should be always active poolSize > 0 aka 1 and more or functions relying on poolmgr will not have pods available the "newdeploy" ones will work without a problem.

      These settings are fine tunnings when choosing between "newdeploy" and "poolmgr" for function creation.
      If newdeploy is set per function this means we are aiming towards scalability and these functions are managed by HPA (Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaling)
      If poolmgr is set per function this means we are aiming towards hot containers(pods) always waiting for function attachment and execution of the requests
      After one pod is associated with a function new one "empty" spawns to wait for another execution if function CPU and Memory are too high it will associate new pod to spawn the function

fields.name: maxPods
fields.description:
Hard cap on the TOTAL number of "poolmgr" pods this environment may have at once:
      the warm pool (poolSize) plus every specialized (function) pod across all functions in it.
      Once the cap is reached the executor refuses to specialize a new pod and the invocation
      fails fast with HTTP 429 instead of provisioning more pods. This prevents a flood of
      invocations (e.g. a misconfigured KEDA/message-queue trigger) from provisioning unbounded
      pods and exhausting the cluster.
      0 (the default) means unlimited. Only applies to "poolmgr" functions ("newdeploy" is already
      bounded by its own HPA maxScale). Should be >= poolSize.

fields.name: builderPoolSize
fields.description: Maximum number of builder pods for this environment. Builder pods are provisioned on demand (one per concurrent build) up to this cap, then scaled back to zero when idle. Building one lambda uses one pod regardless of this value. Default is 1

fields.name: builderMaxParallelBuilds
fields.description: Builds a single builder pod will accept (MAX_PARALLEL_BUILDS). Default is 1 (one build per pod); independent of builderPoolSize

fields.name: builderIdleTimeout
fields.description: Seconds a builder pod stays up after its last build before scaling to zero. 0 = never scale down. Default is 600 (10 minutes)

This is the script which will be executed on build job before lambda initialization

**** START SCRIPT ****

fields.name: scaleOptions
fields.description:
Default scale options for "poolmgr" are these and are defined in JSON 
        {
            "minCpu": 0,
            "maxCpu": 0,
            "minMemory": 0,
            "maxMemory": 0,
            "minScale": 0,
            "maxScale": 0,
            "targetCpu": 0,
            "executorType": "poolmgr",
            "concurrency": 1,
            "functionTimeout": 60,
            "idleTimeout": 120,
            "specializationTimeout": 120
            "retainPods": 0,
            "requestPerPod": 1000
        }
        IMPORTANT: When "executorType" is set to "poolmgr" minScale,maxScale,targetCpu,minCpu,maxCpu,minMemory,maxMemory are DISABLED for EDIT and should ALWAYS be 0!
        IMPORTANT: When "executorType" is set to "poolmgr" these settings are defined inside the Environment Pool instead and managed by the pool not per lambda
        "scaleOptions" field can be left null and it will default to specific values

fields.name: add_knowledge
fields.description:
Add a new node to the knowledge graph.
          Use this to PROACTIVELY save useful information, especially:
          1. **Code Snippets**: If the user says "I like this code", save it as a 'CodeSnippet'.
          2. **Notes**: General facts or preferences.
          3. **Concepts**: Abstract ideas or definitions.

          Common labels: CodeSnippet, Note, Concept, Document.
          IMPORTANT: An 'id' (UUID) is automatically generated if not provided.
          Recommended: Always provide a 'name' property for easier human-readable search.
          Auto-Embedding: The content will be automatically embedded for vector search.

args.description: The label for the node (e.g. Concept, CodeSnippet)

args.name: properties
args.description: Key-value pairs for the node properties. Ensure text content is in a property like "text", "description", or "content" for best embedding.

fields.name: save_project_memory

Save a fact/snippet/preference to THIS PROJECT'S shared memory
          (visible to everyone with access to the project).
          Use this CONSERVATIVELY — only when the user explicitly asks to remember
          something, praises code YOU generated, or states a durable
          project-specific decision/preference clearly worth recalling later.
          ASK before saving unless the user already told you to. ALWAYS pass the
          projectId from your context. (Global knowledge is admin-only.)

args.name: projectId
args.description: The project id to save this memory under — pass your current projectId from context.

args.name: label
args.description: The label for the node (e.g. Concept, CodeSnippet, Note)

args.name: properties

fields.name: executeCode
fields.description: Run JavaScript in a fresh, isolated, resource-limited QuickJS (WASM) sandbox and return its result, console output, timing and any error. Supports a per-run in-memory virtual filesystem (multi-file ES modules + node:fs via options.files) and Programmatic Tool Calling via the awaitable `tools.*` namespace. Built for AI agents to write and verify code before deploying it. Stateless by default (nothing persisted between calls); with workspace persistence enabled, options.projectId + options.workdir target a durable server-side workspace instead (call the metadata query for the contract).

args.name: code
args.description: The code to run. Snippet mode (no options.files): the body of an async function — use `return <value>` for `result` (no return -> null), top-level `await` works. Project mode (options.files given): an ES module — use `export default <value>` for `result`, `import` the mounted files, and node:fs via NAMED imports; ignored if options.entrypoint names the entry file (pass "" then). Call allowlisted tools as `await tools.<name>(args)`; `console.*` is captured in `logs`. Non-JSON-serializable results (functions, undefined, symbols, BigInt) come back as null. Example (snippet): `console.log("hi"); return 1 + 1` -> 2.

args.name: options
args.description: Optional JSON. `files`: a { path: content } map to mount as an in-memory project (switches to project mode; returned afterwards as `changedFiles`). `entrypoint`: which mounted file to run as the entry module. `env`: key/values exposed as the `env` global. `tools`: allowlist of host tool names this run may call, e.g. ["httpGet"] (disabled unless named). `projectId` + `workdir` (both together; needs workspace persistence enabled — see the metadata query): run against that durable workspace instead — its files are hydrated into the sandbox, `files` becomes an ephemeral overlay, and after a successful run the changes are persisted back (`changedFiles` is then only the delta; see `persistence`). Limits (clamped to operator ceilings): `timeoutMs` (CPU budget, excludes tool I/O), `overallTimeoutMs` (total wall-clock), `memoryLimitBytes`, `maxStackSizeBytes`.

inputFields.name: model
inputFields.description: ID of the model to use. You can use the [List models](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/models/list) API to see all of your available models, or see our [Model overview](/docs/models/overview) for descriptions of them.

inputFields.name: max_tokens
inputFields.description: The maximum number of [tokens](/tokenizer) to generate in the completion.  The token count of your prompt plus `max_tokens` cannot exceed the model's context length. Most models have a context length of 2048 tokens (except for the newest models, which support 4096).

inputFields.name: suffix
inputFields.description: The suffix that comes after a completion of inserted text.

inputFields.name: temperature
inputFields.description: What [sampling temperature](https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-sample-from-language-models-682bceb97277) to use. Higher values means the model will take more risks. Try 0.9 for more creative applications, and 0 (argmax sampling) for ones with a well-defined answer.  We generally recommend altering this or `top_p` but not both.

inputFields.name: top_p
inputFields.description: An alternative to sampling with temperature, called nucleus sampling, where the model considers the results of the tokens with top_p probability mass. So 0.1 means only the tokens comprising the top 10% probability mass are considered.  We generally recommend altering this or `temperature` but not both.

inputFields.name: n
inputFields.description: How many completions to generate for each prompt.  **Note:** Because this parameter generates many completions, it can quickly consume your token quota. Use carefully and ensure that you have reasonable settings for `max_tokens` and `stop`.

inputFields.name: logprobs
inputFields.description: Include the log probabilities on the `logprobs` most likely tokens, as well the chosen tokens. For example, if `logprobs` is 5, the API will return a list of the 5 most likely tokens. The API will always return the `logprob` of the sampled token, so there may be up to `logprobs+1` elements in the response.  The maximum value for `logprobs` is 5. If you need more than this, please contact us through our [Help center](https://help.openai.com) and describe your use case.

inputFields.name: presence_penalty
inputFields.description: Number between -2.0 and 2.0. Positive values penalize new tokens based on whether they appear in the text so far, increasing the model's likelihood to talk about new topics.  [See more information about frequency and presence penalties.](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/parameter-details)

inputFields.name: frequency_penalty
inputFields.description: Number between -2.0 and 2.0. Positive values penalize new tokens based on their existing frequency in the text so far, decreasing the model's likelihood to repeat the same line verbatim.  [See more information about frequency and presence penalties.](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/parameter-details)

inputFields.name: best_of
inputFields.description: Generates `best_of` completions server-side and returns the "best" (the one with the highest log probability per token). Results cannot be streamed.  When used with `n`, `best_of` controls the number of candidate completions and `n` specifies how many to return – `best_of` must be greater than `n`.  **Note:** Because this parameter generates many completions, it can quickly consume your token quota. Use carefully and ensure that you have reasonable settings for `max_tokens` and `stop`.

types.name: ExecutionResult
types.description: Outcome of one sandboxed code execution: the returned value, captured console output, timing, and any error.

fields.name: success
fields.description: True when the code ran to completion; false when it threw, failed to compile, or hit the time/memory limit.

fields.name: result
fields.description: The value the code returned, as native JSON (number, string, boolean, object, array or null). Null when the code did not `return` anything, or on failure. Non-serializable values (functions, undefined, symbols, BigInt) appear as null.

fields.name: error
fields.description: When `success` is false, `{ name, message, stack? }` describing what went wrong (e.g. a thrown error, a SyntaxError, or `interrupted` on timeout).

fields.name: logs
fields.description: Everything the sandbox wrote to console.{log,info,warn,error,debug}, in order, each line prefixed with its level.

fields.name: executionTimeMs
fields.description: Wall-clock duration of the run in milliseconds (includes time spent awaiting host tool calls).

fields.name: changedFiles
fields.description: Project mode only (when `options.files` was provided): a `{ path: content }` map of the virtual filesystem after the run — every file present at the end, including ones the code wrote via `node:fs`. Null in snippet mode. The filesystem is in-memory and discarded after the run; this snapshot is the only way to read back what the code produced. In workspace mode (options.projectId + options.workdir) this is instead the DELTA: only files the run created or modified relative to the workspace.

fields.name: changedFilesTruncated
fields.description: True when the `changedFiles` snapshot hit the operator byte ceiling and files were dropped from it — treat the map as incomplete, never as evidence a missing file was deleted.

fields.name: persistence
fields.description: Workspace mode only (options.projectId + options.workdir with persistence enabled): `{ projectId, workdir, persistedFiles: [path], deletedFiles: [path], skippedDeletionCheck: boolean }` describing what was written back to durable storage after the run. Null in stateless runs.

types.name: __Schema
types.description: A GraphQL Schema defines the capabilities of a GraphQL server. It exposes all available types and directives on the server, as well as the entry points for query, mutation, and subscription operations.

fields.name: types
fields.description: A list of all types supported by this server.

fields.name: queryType
fields.description: The type that query operations will be rooted at.

fields.name: mutationType
fields.description: If this server supports mutation, the type that mutation operations will be rooted at.

fields.name: subscriptionType
fields.description: If this server support subscription, the type that subscription operations will be rooted at.

fields.name: directives
fields.description: A list of all directives supported by this server.

types.name: __Type
types.description:
The fundamental unit of any GraphQL Schema is the type. There are many kinds of types in GraphQL as represented by the `__TypeKind` enum.

Depending on the kind of a type, certain fields describe information about that type. Scalar types provide no information beyond a name and description, while Enum types provide their values. Object and Interface types provide the fields they describe. Abstract types, Union and Interface, provide the Object types possible at runtime. List and NonNull types compose other types.

types.name: __TypeKind
types.description: An enum describing what kind of type a given `__Type` is.

enumValues.name: SCALAR
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is a scalar.

enumValues.name: OBJECT
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is an object. `fields` and `interfaces` are valid fields.

enumValues.name: INTERFACE
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is an interface. `fields` and `possibleTypes` are valid fields.

enumValues.name: UNION
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is a union. `possibleTypes` is a valid field.

enumValues.name: ENUM
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is an enum. `enumValues` is a valid field.

enumValues.name: INPUT_OBJECT
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is an input object. `inputFields` is a valid field.

enumValues.name: LIST
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is a list. `ofType` is a valid field.

enumValues.name: NON_NULL
enumValues.description: Indicates this type is a non-null. `ofType` is a valid field.

types.name: __Field
types.description: Object and Interface types are described by a list of Fields, each of which has a name, potentially a list of arguments, and a return type.

types.name: __InputValue
types.description: Arguments provided to Fields or Directives and the input fields of an InputObject are represented as Input Values which describe their type and optionally a default value.

fields.name: defaultValue
fields.description: A GraphQL-formatted string representing the default value for this input value.

types.name: __EnumValue
types.description: One possible value for a given Enum. Enum values are unique values, not a placeholder for a string or numeric value. However an Enum value is returned in a JSON response as a string.

types.name: __Directive
types.description:
A Directive provides a way to describe alternate runtime execution and type validation behavior in a GraphQL document.

In some cases, you need to provide options to alter GraphQL's execution behavior in ways field arguments will not suffice, such as conditionally including or skipping a field. Directives provide this by describing additional information to the executor.

types.name: __DirectiveLocation
types.description: A Directive can be adjacent to many parts of the GraphQL language, a __DirectiveLocation describes one such possible adjacencies.

enumValues.name: QUERY
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a query operation.

enumValues.name: MUTATION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a mutation operation.

enumValues.name: SUBSCRIPTION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a subscription operation.

enumValues.name: FIELD
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a field.

enumValues.name: FRAGMENT_DEFINITION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a fragment definition.

enumValues.name: FRAGMENT_SPREAD
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a fragment spread.

enumValues.name: INLINE_FRAGMENT
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an inline fragment.

enumValues.name: VARIABLE_DEFINITION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a variable definition.

enumValues.name: SCHEMA
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a schema definition.

enumValues.name: SCALAR
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a scalar definition.

enumValues.name: OBJECT
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an object type definition.

enumValues.name: FIELD_DEFINITION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a field definition.

enumValues.name: ARGUMENT_DEFINITION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an argument definition.

enumValues.name: INTERFACE
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an interface definition.

enumValues.name: UNION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to a union definition.

enumValues.name: ENUM
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an enum definition.

enumValues.name: ENUM_VALUE
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an enum value definition.

enumValues.name: INPUT_OBJECT
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an input object type definition.

enumValues.name: INPUT_FIELD_DEFINITION
enumValues.description: Location adjacent to an input object field definition.

directives.name: include
directives.description: Directs the executor to include this field or fragment only when the `if` argument is true.

args.name: if
args.description: Included when true.

directives.name: skip
directives.description: Directs the executor to skip this field or fragment when the `if` argument is true.

args.name: if
args.description: Skipped when true.

directives.name: deprecated
directives.description: Marks an element of a GraphQL schema as no longer supported.

args.name: reason
args.description: Explains why this element was deprecated, usually also including a suggestion for how to access supported similar data. Formatted using the Markdown syntax (as specified by [CommonMark](https://commonmark.org/).
